title: SQL Views and Reusable Queries
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and practical behaviour of SQL Views and Reusable Queries.
Identify which database engine or application layer performs the operation.
Predict the result of the SQLite examples before running them.
Recognize security, recovery, portability and operational limitations.
Apply the concept safely in a realistic database workflow.

understand.concept: A view is a named query exposed like a virtual table. A normal SQLite view stores its SELECT definition rather than a separate copy of the result rows. Views can simplify repeated queries and expose selected columns, but they do not automatically provide authorization or guarantee performance.
understand.whyItMatters: Views can present consistent reporting logic, hide irrelevant columns from application queries and make complex joins easier to reuse.
understand.analogy: Think of a database workflow as a carefully controlled service desk: each operation has a defined responsibility, input and verification step.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model SQL grammar, database transaction isolation, driver APIs, security boundaries or DBMS-specific implementation details.

explain.narrative:
## What a view represents
CREATE VIEW defines a named SELECT statement. Querying the view runs its defining query against the underlying tables; a normal SQLite view does not store a separate result set. Use DROP VIEW to remove it. Some database products support materialized views, but SQLite's ordinary views are not materialized views.

## Creating and using a view
Give views clear names, use explicit column lists and qualify ambiguous columns in joins. A view can be queried with WHERE and ORDER BY like a table. SQLite supports INSTEAD OF triggers for certain writes through views, but simple updatability rules differ across products.

## Security and maintenance
A view is not a substitute for database permissions, parameterized queries or application authorization. Changes to underlying tables can affect dependent views. Test view definitions during schema migrations and avoid SELECT * in long-lived view definitions.

## Worked examples
The five original SQLite examples below are executable in the CodeSaathi SQL Playground. Any host-language API or other DBMS command is explicitly labelled as explanatory rather than runnable.

examples.title: Create a simple view
examples.code: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS active_products; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS view_products; CREATE TABLE view_products(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, active INTEGER); INSERT INTO view_products VALUES(1,'Notebook',1),(2,'Old stock',0); CREATE VIEW active_products AS SELECT id,name FROM view_products WHERE active=1; SELECT id,name FROM active_products;
examples.explanation: A view stores a query definition and returns rows matching its SELECT.

examples.title: Filter a view result
examples.code: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS city_customers; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS view_customers; CREATE TABLE view_customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT); INSERT INTO view_customers VALUES(1,'Asha','Hyderabad'),(2,'Bilal','Vijayawada'); CREATE VIEW city_customers AS SELECT id,name,city FROM view_customers; SELECT name FROM city_customers WHERE city='Hyderabad';
examples.explanation: A view can be queried with ordinary SELECT filtering.

examples.title: Join tables through a view
examples.code: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS order_summary; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS view_orders; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS view_clients; CREATE TABLE view_clients(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,name TEXT); CREATE TABLE view_orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,client_id INTEGER,total INTEGER); INSERT INTO view_clients VALUES(1,'Mira'),(2,'Ravi'); INSERT INTO view_orders VALUES(10,1,250),(11,2,400); CREATE VIEW order_summary AS SELECT o.id, c.name, o.total FROM view_orders o JOIN view_clients c ON c.id=o.client_id; SELECT name,total FROM order_summary ORDER BY total;
examples.explanation: A view can package a join into a reusable named query.

examples.title: Replace a view definition
examples.code: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS product_names; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS view_items; CREATE TABLE view_items(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,name TEXT,price INTEGER); INSERT INTO view_items VALUES(1,'Pen',10),(2,'Book',80); CREATE VIEW product_names AS SELECT name FROM view_items; DROP VIEW product_names; CREATE VIEW product_names AS SELECT name,price FROM view_items; SELECT name,price FROM product_names ORDER BY price;
examples.explanation: SQLite supports dropping and recreating a view; CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW is not SQLite syntax.

examples.title: Inspect a view definition
examples.code: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS view_status; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS view_tasks; CREATE TABLE view_tasks(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,status TEXT); CREATE VIEW view_status AS SELECT status,COUNT(*) AS total FROM view_tasks GROUP BY status; SELECT type,name FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='view' AND name='view_status';
examples.explanation: sqlite_schema contains the stored SQL definition and metadata for views.

practise.guidedTask: Run all five examples for SQL Views and Reusable Queries. Before running each one, state what the statement or application operation does, predict the result and explain any SQLite-specific limitation.
practise.independentTask: Create a small original scenario for SQL Views and Reusable Queries. Write at least five statements or a documented application workflow, include a safety or verification step, and explain which parts are specific to SQLite or another DBMS.
hints: Read the engine and version notes before choosing syntax.
Keep user-provided values separate from SQL command text.
Use explicit names and columns so the operation is easy to review.
Check the result with a SELECT or integrity/health query.
For operational changes, document backup, restore and rollback requirements.

questions.prompt: What does a normal SQLite view store?
options: A separate physical copy of all result rows
questions.explanation: A normal view is a named query, not a materialized result copy.
CREATE VIEW defines the named query.

questions.prompt: How do you remove a view in SQLite?
questions.explanation: DROP VIEW removes the view definition.

questions.prompt: Does a view automatically enforce user authorization?
options: No, permissions and application authorization must be designed separately
Yes, every view encrypts its rows
No, but it always hides every column
questions.answer: No, permissions and application authorization must be designed separately
questions.explanation: A view alone is not an authorization boundary.

questions.prompt: What is a key difference between a normal and materialized view?
options: A materialized view stores results; a normal SQLite view stores a query definition
A normal view always stores a backup
A materialized view cannot be queried
They are identical in every DBMS
questions.answer: A materialized view stores results; a normal SQLite view stores a query definition
questions.explanation: Materialized views persist computed results; ordinary SQLite views do not.
